chapters.title: Dedication. To M. Talleyrand Perigord, Late Bishop of Autun
paragraphs: Sir,

Having read with great pleasure a pamphlet you recently published on national education, I dedicate this volume to you — the first dedication I have ever written — to persuade you to read it carefully. I do this because I think you will understand me, which I do not expect from many of the smug little intellects who will ridicule arguments they cannot answer. But, sir, my respect for your understanding goes further still: I am confident you will not throw my work aside and quickly decide I am wrong simply because you did not see the subject this way yourself. And forgive my frankness, but I must point out that you treated the question too briefly, content to consider it as it had always been considered before, when even the rights of man — not to mention woman — were dismissed as fanciful. So I call on you now to weigh what I have said about the rights of woman and about national education; and I call with the firm tone of human dignity. My arguments, sir, are dictated by a disinterested spirit: I plead for my sex, not for myself. Independence I have long considered the great blessing of life, the foundation of every virtue; and I will always secure my independence by limiting my wants, even if it means living on a barren heath.

It is, then, my affection for the whole human race that makes my pen race forward to support what I believe to be the cause of virtue; and the same motive makes me earnestly wish to see woman placed in a position where she would advance, not retard, the progress of those glorious principles that give substance to morality. My view on the rights and duties of woman seems to me to follow so naturally from these simple principles that I think it is scarcely possible some of the broad minds who shaped your admirable constitution will not agree with me.

In France, there is undoubtedly a wider diffusion of knowledge than anywhere else in Europe, and I attribute this in large part to the long-standing social mixing of the sexes. I admit freely that in France the very essence of sensuality has been extracted to entertain the voluptuary, and a kind of sentimental lust has prevailed which, combined with the system of duplicity that the whole tone of their political and civil government taught, has given a sinister sort of cleverness to the French character — properly called finesse — and a polish of manners that injures substance by driving sincerity out of society. And modesty, the fairest garment of virtue, has been more grossly insulted in France than even in England, until French women treat as PRUDISH that attention to decency which even brute animals instinctively observe.

Manners and morals are so closely allied that they are often confused; but although manners should be only the natural reflection of morals, when various causes have produced false and corrupt manners, which are picked up very early, morality becomes an empty word. The personal reserve and the sacred respect for cleanliness and delicacy in domestic life, which French women almost despise, are the graceful pillars of modesty; but far from despising these things, if the pure flame of patriotism has reached their hearts, they should work to improve the morals of their fellow citizens — by teaching men not only to respect modesty in women but to acquire it themselves, as the only way to deserve their esteem.

In contending for the rights of women, my main argument rests on this simple principle: that if a woman is not prepared by education to be the companion of man, she will halt the progress of knowledge, for truth must be common to all or it will not effectively shape general practice. And how can woman be expected to cooperate unless she knows why she ought to be virtuous? Unless freedom strengthens her reason until she grasps her duty and sees how it is connected to her real good? If children are to be educated to understand true patriotism, their mother must be a patriot; and the love of humankind, from which an orderly train of virtues springs, can only be produced by considering the moral and civil interest of humankind — but the education and situation of woman, at present, shuts her out from such investigations.

In this work I have produced many arguments, which to me are conclusive, to prove that the prevailing notion of a separate sexual character is subversive of morality. I have argued that to make the human body and mind more perfect, chastity must more universally prevail, and that chastity will never be respected in the male world until the person of a woman is no longer, as it were, idolized when little virtue or sense decorates it with the grand traces of mental beauty or the engaging simplicity of affection.

Consider, sir, dispassionately, these observations, for a glimpse of this truth seemed to open before you when you observed "that to see one half of the human race excluded by the other from all participation of government was a political phenomenon that, according to abstract principles, it was impossible to explain." If that is so, what does your constitution rest on? If the abstract rights of man can bear discussion and explanation, those of woman, by the same reasoning, will not shrink from the same test — though a different opinion prevails in this country, built on the very arguments you use to justify the oppression of woman: prescription.

Consider, I address you as a legislator: when men contend for their freedom, and to be allowed to judge for themselves about their own happiness, is it not inconsistent and unjust to subjugate women, even if you firmly believe you are acting in the manner best calculated to promote their happiness? Who made man the exclusive judge, if woman shares with him the gift of reason?

In this style argue tyrants of every kind, from the weak king to the weak father of a family; they are all eager to crush reason, yet they always insist they usurp its throne only to be useful. Do you not act a similar part when you FORCE all women, by denying them civil and political rights, to remain shut up in their families, groping in the dark? For surely, sir, you will not insist that a duty can be binding which is not founded on reason? If indeed this is their destiny, then arguments may be drawn from reason; and thus solidly supported, the more understanding women acquire, the more attached they will be to their duty, comprehending it — for unless they comprehend it, unless their morals are fixed on the same immutable principles as those of man, no authority can make them discharge it in a virtuous manner. They may be convenient slaves, but slavery will have its constant effect: degrading the master and the abject dependent alike.

But if women are to be excluded, without having a voice, from a participation in the natural rights of mankind, then first prove — to ward off the charge of injustice and inconsistency — that they want reason. Otherwise this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION, the first constitution founded on reason, will forever show that man must, in some shape, act like a tyrant; and tyranny, in whatever part of society it rears its brazen front, will always undermine morality.

I have repeatedly asserted, and produced what seemed to me irrefutable arguments drawn from matters of fact, to prove my claim that women cannot, by force, be confined to domestic concerns. However ignorant they may be, they will meddle in more weighty affairs, neglecting private duties only to disturb, by cunning tricks, the orderly plans of reason which rise above their comprehension.

Besides, while they are only equipped to acquire personal accomplishments, men will seek pleasure in variety, and faithless husbands will make faithless wives; such ignorant beings will indeed be very excusable when, not having been taught to respect the public good and not allowed any civil right, they attempt to do themselves justice by retaliation.
Once this box of mischief has been opened in society, what is left to preserve private virtue, the only security of public freedom and universal happiness?

Let there be, then, no coercion ESTABLISHED in society, and the common law of gravity prevailing, the sexes will fall into their proper places. And now that more equitable laws are shaping your citizens, marriage may become more sacred; your young men may choose wives from motives of affection, and your maidens may allow love to root out vanity.

The father of a family will then not weaken his constitution and debase his sentiments by visiting the harlot, nor forget — in obeying the call of appetite — the purpose for which it was implanted; and the mother will not neglect her children to practice the arts of coquetry, when good sense and modesty secure her the friendship of her husband.

But until men become attentive to the duties of fatherhood, it is in vain to expect women to spend that time in their nurseries which they — "wise in their generation" — choose to spend at their dressing glass; for this exertion of cunning is only an instinct of nature, enabling them to obtain indirectly a little of that power of which they are unjustly denied a share. If women are not permitted to enjoy legitimate rights, they will make both men and themselves vicious in order to obtain illicit privileges.

I wish, sir, to set investigations of this kind afloat in France; and should they lead to a confirmation of my principles, when your constitution is revised, the rights of woman may be respected, if it be fully proved that reason calls for this respect and loudly demands JUSTICE for one half of the human race.
I am, sir,
Yours respectfully,
M. W.

chapters.title: Introduction
paragraphs: After considering the historical record and looking with anxious concern at the living world, I have been pressed down by the most melancholy feelings of sorrowful indignation, and I have sighed when forced to admit that either nature has made a great difference between one man and another, or else the civilization the world has so far achieved has been very partial. I have looked through various books on education and patiently observed the conduct of parents and the management of schools — and what is the result? A deep conviction that the neglected education of my fellow creatures is the great source of the misery I lament; and that women in particular are made weak and wretched by a variety of converging causes, all originating from one hasty conclusion. The conduct and manners of women clearly prove that their minds are not in a healthy state, for, like flowers planted in too rich a soil, their strength and usefulness are sacrificed to beauty; and the flaunting leaves, after having pleased a fastidious eye, fade and are ignored on the stalk long before the season when they ought to have reached maturity. One cause of this barren blooming I attribute to a false system of education, drawn from books written on the subject by men who, considering females as women rather than as human creatures, have been more anxious to make them alluring mistresses than rational wives; and the understanding of the sex has been so taken in by this specious flattery that the civilized women of the present century, with a few exceptions, are only anxious to inspire love, when they ought to cherish a nobler ambition and, by their abilities and virtues, demand respect.

In a treatise on female rights and manners, then, the works that have been written specifically for women's improvement must not be overlooked — especially when the claim is that the minds of women are weakened by false refinement; that the books of instruction written by men of genius have had the same tendency as more frivolous productions; and that, in the true style of Islam, women are only considered as females and not as part of the human species, when improvable reason is supposed to be the dignified distinction that raises men above the brute creation and puts a natural scepter in a feeble hand.

Yet, because I am a woman, I do not want my readers to suppose I mean to violently agitate the contested question of the equality or inferiority of the sex; but since the subject lies in my way and I cannot pass it over without exposing the main tendency of my reasoning to misconstruction, I will stop a moment to state my opinion briefly. In the government of the physical world, it is observable that the female is, in general, inferior to the male. The male pursues, the female yields — this is the law of nature, and it does not appear to be suspended or abrogated in favor of woman. This physical superiority cannot be denied — and it is a noble prerogative! But not content with this natural pre-eminence, men try to sink us still lower, merely to make us alluring objects for a moment; and women, intoxicated by the adoration that men, under the influence of their senses, pay them, do not seek to obtain a lasting interest in their hearts, or to become the friends of the fellow creatures who find amusement in their company.

I am aware of an obvious objection: from every quarter I have heard complaints against masculine women — but where are they to be found? If by this label men mean to inveigh against women's ardor in hunting, shooting, and gaming, I will most cordially join in the cry; but if it is meant against the imitation of manly virtues, or more properly, the attainment of those talents and virtues whose exercise ennobles human character and raises females in the scale of animal being when they are comprehensively termed mankind — all those who view them with a philosophical eye must, I should think, wish with me that they may every day grow more and more masculine.

This discussion naturally divides the subject. I shall first consider women in the grand light of human creatures who, in common with men, are placed on this earth to unfold their faculties; and afterwards I shall more particularly point out their distinct designation.

I also want to steer clear of an error many respectable writers have fallen into; for the instruction that has so far been addressed to women has rather been applicable to LADIES — if we except the little indirect advice scattered through Sandford and Merton. But addressing my sex in a firmer tone, I pay particular attention to those in the middle class, because they appear to be in the most natural state. Perhaps the seeds of false refinement, immorality, and vanity have always been sown by the great. Weak, artificial beings, raised above the common wants and affections of their race in a premature and unnatural manner, undermine the very foundation of virtue and spread corruption through the whole mass of society! As a class of mankind, they have the strongest claim to pity! The education of the rich tends to make them vain and helpless, and the unfolding mind is not strengthened by the practice of those duties that dignify human character. They live only to amuse themselves, and by the same law that in nature invariably produces certain effects, they soon afford only barren amusement.

But since I propose to take a separate view of the different ranks of society and of the moral character of women in each, this hint is sufficient for the present; I have only alluded to the subject because it seems to me to be the very essence of an introduction to give a cursory account of the contents of the work it introduces.

My own sex, I hope, will excuse me if I treat them as rational creatures rather than flattering their FASCINATING graces and viewing them as if they were in a state of perpetual childhood, unable to stand alone. I earnestly wish to point out what true dignity and human happiness consist of — I wish to persuade women to endeavor to acquire strength, both of mind and body, and to convince them that the soft phrases — susceptibility of heart, delicacy of sentiment, refinement of taste — are almost synonyms for weakness, and that those beings who are only the objects of pity and of that kind of love which has been called its sister will soon become objects of contempt.

Dismissing, then, those pretty feminine phrases that men condescendingly use to soften our slavish dependence, and despising that weak elegance of mind, exquisite sensibility, and sweet docility of manners which are supposed to be the sexual characteristics of the weaker vessel, I wish to show that elegance is inferior to virtue, that the first object of laudable ambition is to obtain a character as a human being, regardless of the distinction of sex, and that all secondary aims should be brought to this simple touchstone.

This is a rough sketch of my plan; and should I express my conviction with the energetic feelings I have whenever I think of the subject, the dictates of experience and reflection will be felt by some of my readers. Animated by this important object, I shall scorn to pick my phrases or polish my style — I aim at being useful, and sincerity will keep me unaffected; for wishing rather to persuade by the force of my arguments than to dazzle by the elegance of my language, I shall not waste my time in rounding out periods or fabricating the turgid bombast of artificial feelings which, coming from the head, never reach the heart. I shall be employed about things, not words! And, anxious to make my sex more respectable members of society, I shall try to avoid that flowery diction which has slid from essays into novels, and from novels into familiar letters and conversation.

These pretty nothings, these caricatures of the real beauty of sensibility, dropping glibly from the tongue, spoil the taste and create a kind of sickly delicacy that turns away from simple unadorned truth; and a deluge of false sentiments and overstretched feelings, stifling the natural emotions of the heart, makes insipid the domestic pleasures that ought to sweeten the exercise of those severe duties that educate a rational and immortal being for a nobler field of action.

The education of women has lately been more attended to than formerly; yet they are still reckoned a frivolous sex, and ridiculed or pitied by the writers who try, by satire or instruction, to improve them. It is acknowledged that they spend many of the first years of their lives in acquiring a smattering of accomplishments — meanwhile, strength of body and mind are sacrificed to libertine notions of beauty, to the desire of establishing themselves, the only way women can rise in the world: by marriage. And this desire turning mere animals out of them, when they marry they act as such children may be expected to act: they dress; they paint; and they nickname God's creatures. Surely these weak beings are only fit for the seraglio! Can they govern a family, or take care of the poor babies they bring into the world?

If then it can be fairly deduced from the present conduct of the sex — from the prevailing fondness for pleasure that takes the place of ambition and those nobler passions which open and enlarge the soul — that the instruction women have received has only tended, together with the structure of civil society, to make them insignificant objects of desire, mere propagators of fools; if it can be proved that in aiming to accomplish them, without cultivating their understandings, they are taken out of their sphere of duties and made ridiculous and useless once the short-lived bloom of beauty is over*, I presume that RATIONAL men will excuse me for trying to persuade them to become more masculine and respectable.
(*Footnote. A lively writer — I cannot recall his name — asks what business women past forty have in the world.)

Indeed the word masculine is only a bugbear: there is little reason to fear that women will acquire too much courage or fortitude, for their apparent inferiority with respect to bodily strength must make them, in some degree, dependent on men in the various relations of life; but why should it be increased by prejudices that give a sex to virtue and confound simple truths with sensual reveries?

Women are, in fact, so much degraded by mistaken notions of female excellence that I do not mean to add a paradox when I assert that this artificial weakness produces a propensity to tyrannize, and gives birth to cunning — the natural opponent of strength — which leads them to play off those contemptible infantile airs that undermine esteem even while they excite desire. Do not foster these prejudices, and women will naturally fall into their subordinate but respectable station in life.

It seems scarcely necessary to say that I am now speaking of the sex in general. Many individuals have more sense than their male relatives; and, since nothing preponderates where there is a constant struggle for equilibrium unless it naturally has more gravity, some women govern their husbands without degrading themselves, because intellect will always govern.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Rights and Involved Duties of Mankind Considered
paragraphs: In the present state of society, it seems necessary to go back to first principles in search of the most simple truths, and to contest every inch of ground with some prevailing prejudice. To clear my way, I must be allowed to ask some plain questions; and the answers will probably appear as unambiguous as the axioms on which reasoning is built — though, when entangled with various motives for action, they are formally contradicted, either by the words or the conduct of men.
In what does man's pre-eminence over the brute creation consist? The answer is as clear as that a half is less than the whole: in Reason.
What quality exalts one being above another? Virtue — we spontaneously reply.
For what purpose were the passions implanted? So that man, by struggling with them, might attain a degree of knowledge denied to the brutes — Experience whispers.

Consequently, the perfection of our nature and our capacity for happiness must be measured by the degree of reason, virtue, and knowledge that distinguishes the individual and directs the laws that bind society; and that from the exercise of reason, knowledge and virtue naturally flow is equally undeniable if mankind is viewed collectively.

With the rights and duties of man thus simplified, it seems almost impertinent to attempt to illustrate truths that appear so incontrovertible — yet such deeply rooted prejudices have clouded reason, and such spurious qualities have assumed the name of virtues, that it is necessary to trace the course of reason as it has been perplexed and entangled in error by various accidental circumstances, comparing the simple axiom with casual deviations.

Men, in general, seem to use their reason to justify prejudices they have imbibed they cannot trace how, rather than to root them out. The mind must be strong that resolutely forms its own principles, for a kind of intellectual cowardice prevails which makes many men shrink from the task or only do it by halves. Yet the imperfect conclusions thus drawn are frequently very plausible, because they are built on partial experience, on just but narrow views.

Going back to first principles, vice skulks, with all its native ugliness, away from close investigation; but a set of shallow reasoners are always exclaiming that these arguments prove too much, and that a measure rotten at the core may still be expedient. Thus expediency is continually contrasted with simple principles, until truth is lost in a mist of words, virtue in forms, and knowledge rendered a sounding nothing by the specious prejudices that assume its name.

That the society is formed in the wisest manner whose constitution is founded on the nature of man strikes, in the abstract, every thinking being so forcibly that it looks like presumption to attempt to bring forward proofs — though proof must be brought, or the stronghold of prescription will never be forced by reason; yet to urge prescription as an argument to justify depriving men (or women) of their natural rights is one of the absurd sophisms which daily insult common sense.

The civilization of the bulk of the people of Europe is very partial — indeed, it may be questioned whether they have acquired any virtues, in exchange for innocence, equivalent to the misery produced by the vices that have been plastered over unsightly ignorance, and the freedom which has been bartered for splendid slavery. The desire of dazzling by riches — the most certain pre-eminence a man can obtain — the pleasure of commanding flattering sycophants, and many other complicated low calculations of doting self-love, have all helped overwhelm the mass of mankind and make liberty a convenient handle for mock patriotism. For while rank and titles are held to be of the utmost importance, before which Genius "must hide its diminished head," it is, with a few exceptions, very unfortunate for a nation when a man of abilities, without rank or property, pushes himself forward to notice. Alas! what unheard-of misery have thousands suffered to purchase a cardinal's hat for some intriguing obscure adventurer who longed to be ranked with princes, or to lord it over them by seizing the triple crown!

Such, indeed, has been the wretchedness that has flowed from hereditary honors, riches, and monarchy that men of lively sensibility have almost uttered blasphemy in order to justify the dispensations of providence. Man has been described as independent of the power that made him, or as a lawless planet darting from its orbit to steal the celestial fire of reason; and the vengeance of heaven, lurking in the subtle flame, sufficiently punished his temerity by introducing evil into the world.

Impressed by this view of the misery and disorder that pervaded society, and fatigued with jostling against artificial fools, Rousseau became enamored of solitude; and, being at the same time an optimist, he labors with uncommon eloquence to prove that man was naturally a solitary animal. Misled by his respect for the goodness of God, who certainly — for what man of sense and feeling can doubt it — gave life only to communicate happiness, he considers evil as positive and the work of man, not aware that he was exalting one attribute at the expense of another equally necessary to divine perfection.

Reared on a false hypothesis, his arguments in favor of a state of nature are plausible but unsound. I say unsound, for to assert that a state of nature is preferable to civilization in all its possible perfection is, in other words, to arraign supreme wisdom; and the paradoxical exclamation that God has made all things right, and that evil has been introduced by the creature whom he formed, knowing what he formed, is as unphilosophical as it is impious.

When that wise Being who created us and placed us here saw the fair idea, he willed, by allowing it to be so, that the passions should unfold our reason, because he could see that present evil would produce future good. Could the helpless creature he called from nothing break loose from his providence and boldly learn to know good by practicing evil without his permission? No. How could that energetic advocate for immortality argue so inconsistently? Had mankind remained forever in the brutal state of nature, which even his magic pen cannot paint as a state in which a single virtue took root, it would have been clear, though not to the sensitive unreflecting wanderer, that man was born to run the circle of life and death and to adorn God's garden for some purpose which could not easily be reconciled with his attributes.

But if, to crown the whole, there were to be rational creatures produced, allowed to rise in excellence by the exercise of powers implanted for that purpose — if benignity itself thought fit to call into existence a creature above the brutes, who could think and improve himself — why should that inestimable gift (for a gift it was, if a man was so created as to have a capacity to rise above the state in which sensation produced brutal ease) be called, in direct terms, a curse? A curse it might be reckoned, if all our existence were bounded by our continuance in this world; for why should the gracious fountain of life give us passions and the power of reflection, only to embitter our days and inspire us with mistaken notions of dignity? Why should he lead us from love of ourselves to the sublime emotions that the discovery of his wisdom and goodness excites, if these feelings were not set in motion to improve our nature, of which they make a part, and to render us capable of enjoying a more godlike portion of happiness? Firmly persuaded that no evil exists in the world which God did not design to take place, I build my belief on the perfection of God.
Rousseau exerts himself to prove that all WAS right originally; a crowd of authors that all IS now right; and I, that all WILL BE right.

But, true to his first position, next to a state of nature Rousseau celebrates barbarism, and, apostrophizing the shade of Fabricius, he forgets that, in conquering the world, the Romans never dreamed of establishing their own liberty on a firm basis, or of extending the reign of virtue. Eager to support his system, he stigmatizes as vicious every effort of genius; and, uttering the apotheosis of savage virtues, he exalts to demigods those who were scarcely human — the brutal Spartans, who in defiance of justice and gratitude sacrificed in cold blood the slaves who had shown themselves men by rescuing their oppressors.

Disgusted with artificial manners and virtues, the citizen of Geneva, instead of properly sifting the subject, threw away the wheat with the chaff, without waiting to inquire whether the evils his ardent soul turned from indignantly were the consequence of civilization or the vestiges of barbarism. He saw vice trampling on virtue, and the semblance of goodness taking the place of the reality; he saw talents bent by power to sinister purposes, and never thought of tracing the gigantic mischief back to arbitrary power, back to the hereditary distinctions that clash with the mental superiority which naturally raises a man above his fellows. He did not perceive that the regal power, in a few generations, introduces idiocy into the noble stem, and holds out baits to render thousands idle and vicious.

Nothing can set the regal character in a more contemptible point of view than the various crimes that have elevated men to the supreme dignity. Vile intrigues, unnatural crimes, and every vice that degrades our nature have been the steps to this distinguished eminence; yet millions of men have supinely allowed the nerveless limbs of the posterity of such rapacious prowlers to rest quietly on their bloodstained thrones.

What but a pestilential vapor can hover over society when its chief director is only instructed in the invention of crimes, or the stupid routine of childish ceremonies? Will men never be wise? Will they never cease to expect corn from tares, and figs from thistles?

It is impossible for any man, when the most favorable circumstances concur, to acquire sufficient knowledge and strength of mind to discharge the duties of a king entrusted with uncontrolled power; how then must these duties be violated when his very elevation is an insuperable bar to the attainment of either wisdom or virtue — when all the feelings of a man are stifled by flattery, and reflection shut out by pleasure! Surely it is madness to make the fate of thousands depend on the caprice of a weak fellow creature, whose very station sinks him NECESSARILY below the meanest of his subjects! But one power should not be thrown down to exalt another — for all power intoxicates weak man; and its abuse proves that the more equality there is established among men, the more virtue and happiness will reign in society. But this, and any similar maxim deduced from simple reason, raises an outcry — the church or the state is in danger if faith in the wisdom of antiquity is not implicit; and they who, roused by the sight of human calamity, dare to attack human authority, are reviled as despisers of God and enemies of man. These are bitter calumnies, yet they reached one of the best of men, (Dr. Price,) whose ashes still preach peace, and whose memory demands a respectful pause when subjects are discussed that lay so near his heart.

After attacking the sacred majesty of kings, I shall scarcely excite surprise by adding my firm conviction that every profession in which great subordination of rank constitutes its power is highly injurious to morality.

A standing army, for instance, is incompatible with freedom, because subordination and rigor are the very sinews of military discipline; and despotism is necessary to give vigor to enterprises that one will directs. A spirit inspired by romantic notions of honor — a kind of morality founded on the fashion of the age — can only be felt by a few officers, while the main body must be moved by command, like the waves of the sea; for the strong wind of authority pushes the crowd of subalterns forward, they scarcely know or care why, with headlong fury.

Besides, nothing can be so prejudicial to the morals of the inhabitants of country towns as the occasional residence of a set of idle superficial young men whose only occupation is gallantry, and whose polished manners make vice more dangerous by concealing its deformity under gay ornamental drapery. An air of fashion — which is but a badge of slavery, and proves that the soul has not a strong individual character — awes simple country people into an imitation of the vices, when they cannot catch the slippery graces of politeness. Every corps is a chain of despots who, submitting and tyrannizing without exercising their reason, become dead weights of vice and folly on the community. A man of rank or fortune, sure of rising by interest, has nothing to do but pursue some extravagant freak; while the needy GENTLEMAN, who is to rise, as the phrase turns, by his merit, becomes a servile parasite or vile pander.

Sailors, the naval gentlemen, come under the same description, only their vices assume a different and coarser cast. They are more positively indolent when not discharging the ceremonials of their station, while the insignificant fluttering of soldiers may be termed active idleness. More confined to the society of men, the former acquire a fondness for humor and mischievous tricks; while the latter, mixing frequently with well-bred women, catch a sentimental cant. But mind is equally out of the question, whether they indulge the horse-laugh or the polite simper.

May I be allowed to extend the comparison to a profession where more mind is certainly to be found, for the clergy have superior opportunities of improvement, though subordination almost equally cramps their faculties? The blind submission imposed at college to forms of belief serves as a noviciate to the curate, who most obsequiously respects the opinion of his rector or patron, if he means to rise in his profession. Perhaps there cannot be a more forcible contrast than between the servile, dependent gait of a poor curate and the courtly mien of a bishop. And the respect and contempt they inspire render the discharge of their separate functions equally useless.

It is of great importance to observe that the character of every man is, in some degree, formed by his profession. A man of sense may only have a cast of countenance that wears off as you trace his individuality, while the weak, common man has scarcely ever any character but what belongs to the body; at least, all his opinions have been so steeped in the vat consecrated by authority that the faint spirit which the grape of his own vine yields cannot be distinguished.
Society, therefore, as it becomes more enlightened, should be very careful not to establish bodies of men who must necessarily be made foolish or vicious by the very constitution of their profession.

In the infancy of society, when men were just emerging out of barbarism, chiefs and priests, touching the most powerful springs of savage conduct — hope and fear — must have had unbounded sway. An aristocracy, of course, is naturally the first form of government. But clashing interests soon losing their equipoise, a monarchy and hierarchy break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles, and the foundation of both is secured by feudal tenures. This appears to be the origin of monarchical and priestly power, and the dawn of civilization. But such combustible materials cannot long be pent up; and, getting vent in foreign wars and internal insurrections, the people acquire some power in the tumult, which obliges their rulers to gloss over their oppression with a show of right. Thus, as wars, agriculture, commerce, and literature expand the mind, despots are compelled to make covert corruption hold fast the power which was formerly snatched by open force.* And this baneful lurking gangrene is most quickly spread by luxury and superstition, the sure dregs of ambition. The indolent puppet of a court first becomes a luxurious monster, or fastidious sensualist, and then makes the contagion that his unnatural state spreads the instrument of tyranny.

(*Footnote. Men of abilities scatter seeds that grow up and have a great influence on the forming opinion; and when once the public opinion preponderates through the exertion of reason, the overthrow of arbitrary power is not very distant.)

It is the pestiferous purple that renders the progress of civilization a curse, and warps the understanding until men of sensibility doubt whether the expansion of intellect produces a greater portion of happiness or misery. But the nature of the poison points out the antidote; and had Rousseau mounted one step higher in his investigation, or could his eye have pierced through the foggy atmosphere which he almost disdained to breathe, his active mind would have darted forward to contemplate the perfection of man in the establishment of true civilization, instead of taking his ferocious flight back to the night of sensual ignorance.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Prevailing Opinion of a Sexual Character Discussed
paragraphs: To account for and excuse the tyranny of man, many ingenious arguments have been put forward to prove that the two sexes, in acquiring virtue, ought to aim at very different characters: or, to speak plainly, women are not allowed enough strength of mind to acquire what really deserves the name of virtue. Yet it should seem, granting that they have souls, that providence has appointed only one path leading MANKIND to either virtue or happiness.

If, then, women are not a swarm of ephemeron triflers, why should they be kept in ignorance under the specious name of innocence? Men complain, and with reason, of the follies and caprices of our sex, when they are not bitterly satirizing our headstrong passions and groveling vices. Behold, I should answer, the natural effect of ignorance! The mind will always be unstable when it has only prejudices to rest on, and the current will run with destructive fury when there are no barriers to break its force. Women are told from infancy, and taught by their mothers' example, that a little knowledge of human weakness—justly called cunning—softness of temper, OUTWARD obedience, and scrupulous attention to a childish kind of propriety will earn them the protection of man; and if they are beautiful, nothing else is needed for at least twenty years of their lives.

This is how Milton describes our first frail mother; though when he tells us that women are formed for softness and sweet attractive grace, I cannot grasp his meaning, unless in the true Mahometan strain he meant to deprive us of souls, and to imply that we were beings designed only by sweet attractive grace, and docile blind obedience, to gratify the senses of man when he can no longer soar on the wing of contemplation.

How grossly they insult us, those who advise us only to make ourselves gentle, domestic brutes! Take, for instance, the winning softness so warmly and frequently recommended, that governs by obeying. What childish expressions! And how insignificant is the being—can it possibly be immortal?—who will condescend to govern by such sinister methods! “Certainly,” says Lord Bacon, “man is of kin to the beasts by his body: and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit, he is a base and ignoble creature!” Men, indeed, seem to me to act in a very unphilosophical manner when they try to secure women’s good conduct by keeping them always in a state of childhood. Rousseau was more consistent when he wished to halt the progress of reason in both sexes; for if men eat from the tree of knowledge, women will come in for a taste: but from the imperfect cultivation their understandings now receive, all they gain is a knowledge of evil.

Children, I grant, should be innocent; but when the word is applied to men or women, it is only a polite term for weakness. For if it is granted that women were destined by Providence to acquire human virtues, and through the exercise of their understandings to develop that stability of character which is the firmest ground for our future hopes, then they must be allowed to turn toward the fountain of light, and not forced to shape their course by the twinkling of a mere satellite. Milton, I grant, held a very different opinion; for he bows only to the indefeasible right of beauty, though it would be difficult to reconcile two passages I now mean to contrast: but great men are often led into similar inconsistencies by their senses:—

“To whom thus Eve with perfect beauty adorned: My author and disposer, what thou bidst Unargued I obey; so God ordains; God is thy law, thou mine; to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge and her praise.”

These are exactly the arguments I have used with children; but I have added, “Your reason is now gaining strength, and until it reaches some degree of maturity, you must look to me for advice: after that, you ought to THINK, and rely only on God.”
Yet in the following lines Milton seems to agree with me, when he has Adam reason with his Maker:—

“Hast thou not made me here thy substitute, And these inferior far beneath me set? Among unequals what society Can sort, what harmony or delight? Which must be mutual, in proportion due Given and received; but in disparity The one intense, the other still remiss Cannot well suit with either, but soon prove Tedious alike: of fellowship I speak Such as I seek fit to participate All rational delight.”

In discussing the manners of women, then, let us set aside sensual arguments and trace what we should try to make them, so that they may cooperate, if the expression is not too bold, with the Supreme Being.

By individual education I mean—since the sense of the word is not precisely defined—such attention to a child as will slowly sharpen the senses, form the temper, regulate the passions as they begin to ferment, and set the understanding to work before the body reaches maturity; so that the adult may only have to continue, not to begin, the important task of learning to think and reason.

To prevent any misunderstanding, I must add that I do not believe a private education can work the wonders that some optimistic writers have attributed to it. Men and women must be educated, to a great degree, by the opinions and manners of the society they live in. In every age there has been a stream of popular opinion that has carried everything before it, giving each century what is, in effect, a family character. It may then be fairly inferred that until society is differently constituted, much cannot be expected from education. However, it is enough for my present purpose to assert that, whatever effect circumstances have on abilities, every being can become virtuous through the exercise of its own reason; for if even one being were created with vicious inclinations—that is, positively bad—what could save us from atheism? Or if we still worship a God, is that God not a devil?

Consequently, the most perfect education, in my opinion, is the kind of exercise of the understanding best calculated to strengthen the body and form the heart; in other words, to enable the individual to acquire habits of virtue that will render it independent. In fact, it is a farce to call any being virtuous whose virtues do not result from the exercise of its own reason. This was Rousseau’s opinion about men: I extend it to women, and I confidently assert that they have been drawn out of their sphere by false refinement, not by any attempt to acquire masculine qualities. Still, the regal homage they receive is so intoxicating that, until the manners of the age are changed and built on more reasonable principles, it may be impossible to convince them that the illegitimate power they gain by degrading themselves is a curse, and that they must return to nature and equality if they wish to secure the placid satisfaction that unspoiled affections provide. But for that epoch we must wait—wait, perhaps, until kings and nobles, enlightened by reason and preferring the real dignity of man to childish pomp, throw off their gaudy hereditary trappings; and if even then women do not give up the arbitrary power of beauty, they will prove that they have LESS mind than man. I may be accused of arrogance; still, I must declare what I firmly believe: that all the writers who have written on the subject of female education and manners, from Rousseau to Dr. Gregory, have contributed to making women more artificial and weaker in character than they would otherwise have been, and therefore more useless members of society. I might have expressed this conviction in a lower key, but I am afraid it would have sounded like the whine of affectation, not the faithful expression of my feelings and the clear conclusion that experience and reflection have led me to draw. When I reach that division of the subject, I shall point out the passages I particularly disapprove of in the works of the authors I have just mentioned; but it is first necessary to observe that my objection extends to the whole purpose of those books, which tend, in my opinion, to degrade one half of the human species and render women pleasing at the expense of every solid virtue.

Though to reason on Rousseau’s ground, if man did attain a degree of perfection of mind when his body arrived at maturity, it might be proper, in order to make a man and his wife ONE, that she should rely entirely on his understanding; and the graceful ivy clasping the oak that supported it would form a whole in which strength and beauty would be equally conspicuous. But, alas! Husbands, as well as their helpmates, are often only overgrown children; in fact, thanks to early debauchery, they are scarcely men in their outward form, and if the blind lead the blind, we need no messenger from heaven to tell us the consequence.

Many causes, in the present corrupt state of society, contribute to enslave women by cramping their understandings and sharpening their senses. One that perhaps quietly does more mischief than all the rest is their disregard of order.

To do everything in an orderly manner is a most important precept, which women—who generally receive only a disorderly kind of education—seldom follow with the same exactness that men, broken into method from infancy, observe. This careless guesswork, for what other word can describe the random exertions of a kind of instinctive common sense never tested by reason, prevents them from generalizing matters of fact, so that they do today what they did yesterday merely because they did it yesterday.

This contempt of the understanding in early life has more harmful consequences than is commonly supposed; for the little knowledge that women of strong minds attain is, for various reasons, more scattered than men’s knowledge, and is acquired more from sheer observation of real life than from comparing what has been individually observed with the results of experience generalized by reflection. Drawn by their dependent situation and domestic duties more into society, what they learn comes in snatches; and since learning is generally only a secondary matter for them, they do not pursue any branch with the persevering eagerness needed to give vigor to the faculties and clarity to the judgment. In the present state of society, a little learning is required to support the character of a gentleman, and boys are obliged to submit to a few years of discipline. But in the education of women the cultivation of the understanding is always subordinate to acquiring some bodily accomplishment; even while enervated by confinement and false notions of modesty, the body is prevented from reaching the grace and beauty that relaxed, half-formed limbs can never display. Besides, in youth their faculties are not drawn out by emulation; and with no serious scientific study, if they have natural sagacity it is turned too soon toward life and manners. They dwell on effects and modifications without tracing them back to causes; and complicated rules for adjusting behaviour are a weak substitute for simple principles.

As proof that education gives this appearance of weakness to females, take the example of military men, who, like them, are sent into the world before their minds have been stored with knowledge or fortified by principles. The consequences are similar; soldiers pick up a little superficial knowledge, snatched from the muddy current of conversation, and from constantly mixing in society they gain what is called a knowledge of the world; and this familiarity with manners and customs has frequently been confused with a knowledge of the human heart. But can the crude fruit of casual observation, never tested by judgment formed by comparing speculation and experience, deserve such a distinction? Soldiers, like women, practice the minor virtues with punctilious politeness. Where, then, is the sexual difference, when the education has been the same? All the difference I can detect arises from the superior advantage of liberty, which lets soldiers see more of life.
It is perhaps wandering from my present subject to make a political remark; but as it was naturally produced by the train of my reflections, I shall not pass it over in silence.

Standing armies can never be composed of resolute, robust men; they may be well-disciplined machines, but they will rarely contain men under the influence of strong passions or with truly vigorous faculties. As for any depth of understanding, I will venture to say it is as rarely found in the army as among women; and I maintain the cause is the same. It may also be noted that officers are particularly attentive to their persons, fond of dancing, crowded rooms, adventures, and ridicule. Like the FAIR sex, the business of their lives is gallantry. They were taught to please, and they live only to please. Yet they do not lose their rank in the distinction between the sexes, for they are still reckoned superior to women, though in what their superiority consists, beyond what I have just mentioned, is hard to discover.

The great misfortune is this: that both acquire manners before morals, and a knowledge of life before they have, through reflection, any acquaintance with the grand ideal outline of human nature. The consequence is natural; satisfied with common nature, they become prey to prejudices, and taking all their opinions on credit, they blindly submit to authority. So that if they have any sense, it is a kind of instinctive glance that catches proportions and decides about manners; but it fails when arguments must be pursued below the surface, or opinions analyzed.

May not the same remark be applied to women? Indeed, the argument can be carried still further, for both are thrown out of any useful station by the unnatural distinctions established in civilized life. Riches and hereditary honours have turned women into cyphers, used only to give consequence to the numerical figure; and idleness has produced a mixture of gallantry and despotism in society which leads the very men who are slaves to their mistresses to tyrannize over their sisters, wives, and daughters. This, it is true, only keeps them in rank and file. Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end of blind obedience; but as blind obedience is what power always seeks, tyrants and sensualists are right to keep women in the dark, since the former want only slaves, and the latter only a plaything. The sensualist has indeed been the most dangerous of tyrants, and women have been duped by their lovers as princes have been by their ministers, while dreaming that they reigned over them.

I now mainly allude to Rousseau, for his character of Sophia is undoubtedly captivating, though it strikes me as grossly unnatural. However, it is not the superstructure but the foundation of her character—the principles on which her education was built—that I mean to attack. Indeed, much as I admire the genius of that able writer, whose opinions I shall often have occasion to cite, indignation always takes the place of admiration, and the rigid frown of insulted virtue effaces the smile of complacency his eloquent passages tend to raise, when I read his voluptuous reveries. Is this the man who, in his ardour for virtue, would banish all the soft arts of peace and almost carry us back to Spartan discipline? Is this the man who delights in painting the useful struggles of passion, the triumphs of good dispositions, and the heroic flights that carry the glowing soul out of itself? How are these mighty sentiments lowered when he describes the pretty foot and enticing airs of his little favourite! But for now I waive the subject; instead of severely reproving the passing effusions of overweening sensibility, I shall only observe that anyone who has cast a benevolent eye on society must often have been gratified by the sight of humble mutual love, not dignified by sentiment nor strengthened by union in intellectual pursuits. The domestic trifles of the day have provided matter for cheerful conversation, and innocent caresses have softened toils that required no great exercise of mind or stretch of thought; yet has not the sight of this moderate happiness excited more tenderness than respect? An emotion similar to what we feel when children are playing or animals are sporting, while the contemplation of the noble struggles of suffering merit has raised admiration and carried our thoughts to that world where sensation will give place to reason.
Women, therefore, are to be considered either as moral beings, or as so weak that they must be entirely subjected to the superior faculties of men.

Let us examine this question. Rousseau declares that a woman should never, for a moment, feel herself independent; that she should be governed by fear to exercise her NATURAL cunning, and made a coquettish slave in order to be a more alluring object of desire, a SWEETER companion to man whenever he chooses to relax himself. He carries the arguments he pretends to draw from the indications of nature still further, and insinuates that truth and fortitude, the cornerstones of all human virtue, must be cultivated with certain restrictions, because in the female character obedience is the grand lesson that should be impressed with unrelenting rigour.

What nonsense! When will a great man arise with enough strength of mind to puff away the fumes that pride and sensuality have spread over the subject? If women are by nature inferior to men, their virtues must still be the same in kind, if not in degree, or else virtue is a relative idea; consequently, their conduct should be founded on the same principles and have the same aim.

Connected with man as daughters, wives, and mothers, their moral character may be judged by how they fulfill those simple duties; but the end, the grand end of their exertions, should be to unfold their own faculties and acquire the dignity of conscious virtue. They may try to make their road pleasant, but should never forget, like men, that life does not yield the happiness that can satisfy an immortal soul. I do not mean to insinuate that either sex should be so lost in abstract reflections or distant views as to forget the affections and duties before them, which are in truth the means appointed to produce the fruit of life; on the contrary, I warmly recommend them, even while I assert that they afford the most satisfaction when considered in their true subordinate light.

The prevailing opinion that woman was created for man probably has its origin in Moses’s poetical story; yet since very few who have given serious thought to the subject have ever supposed that Eve was, literally speaking, one of Adam’s ribs, the deduction must be allowed to fall apart—or be admitted only so far as it proves that man, from the remotest antiquity, found it convenient to use his strength to subjugate his companion, and his ingenuity to show that her neck ought to be bent under the yoke, because she, like the brute creation, was created to do his pleasure.

Let it not be concluded that I wish to invert the order of things; I have already granted that, from the constitution of their bodies, men seem to be designed by Providence to attain a greater degree of virtue. I speak collectively of the whole sex; but I see no shadow of a reason to conclude that their virtues should differ in nature. In fact, how can they, if virtue has only one eternal standard? I must therefore, if I reason consistently, maintain as strongly that they have the same simple direction, as that there is a God.

It follows, then, that cunning should not be set against wisdom, little cares against great exertions, or insipid softness, varnished over with the name of gentleness, against that fortitude which only grand views can inspire.

I shall be told that woman would then lose many of her peculiar graces, and the opinion of a well-known poet might be quoted to refute my unqualified claims. For Pope has said, in the name of the whole male sex,
“Yet ne’er so sure our passions to create, As when she touch’d the brink of all we hate.”

In what light this sally places men and women, I leave to the judicious to determine; meanwhile, I shall content myself with observing that I cannot see why, unless they are mortal, females should always be degraded by being made subservient to love or lust.

To speak disrespectfully of love is, I know, high treason against sentiment and fine feelings; but I wish to speak the plain language of truth, and to address the head rather than the heart. To try to reason love out of the world would be to out-Quixote Cervantes, and would equally offend against common sense; but to try to restrain this tumultuous passion, and to prove that it should not be allowed to dethrone superior powers or to usurp the sceptre that the understanding should always coolly wield, seems less wild.

Youth is the season for love in both sexes; but in those days of thoughtless enjoyment, provision should be made for the more important years of life, when reflection takes the place of sensation. But Rousseau, and most of the male writers who have followed his lead, have warmly insisted that the whole tendency of female education ought to be directed to one point—to render women pleasing.

Let me reason with the supporters of this opinion, those with any knowledge of human nature: do they imagine that marriage can root out the habit of life? The woman who has only been taught to please will soon find that her charms are oblique sunbeams, and that they cannot have much effect on her husband’s heart when seen every day, once summer is past and gone. Will she then have enough native energy to look into herself for comfort and cultivate her dormant faculties? Or is it not more reasonable to expect that she will try to please other men, and in the excitement of the prospect of new conquests, try to forget the mortification her love or pride has received? When the husband ceases to be a lover—and the time will inevitably come—her desire to please will then grow languid, or become a spring of bitterness; and love, perhaps the most fleeting of all passions, gives way to jealousy or vanity.

I am speaking now of women restrained by principle or prejudice; such women, though they would shrink from an intrigue with real abhorrence, still wish to be convinced by the homage of gallantry that they are cruelly neglected by their husbands; or days and weeks are spent in daydreaming of the happiness enjoyed by congenial souls, until health is undermined and spirits broken by discontent. How then can the great art of pleasing be such a necessary study? It is only useful to a mistress; the chaste wife and serious mother should regard her power to please merely as the polish of her virtues, and her husband’s affection as one of the comforts that make her task less difficult and her life happier. But whether she is loved or neglected, her first wish should be to make herself respectable, and not rely for all her happiness on a being subject to the same infirmities as herself.
The amiable Dr. Gregory fell into a similar error. I respect his heart, but I entirely disapprove of his celebrated Legacy to his Daughters.

He advises them to cultivate a fondness for dress, because a fondness for dress, he claims, is natural to them. I am unable to understand what either he or Rousseau means when they frequently use this vague term. If they were telling us that in a pre-existent state the soul was fond of dress and brought this inclination with it into a new body, I would listen with a half-smile, as I often do when I hear someone rant about innate elegance. But if all he meant was that the exercise of the faculties produces this fondness, I deny it. It is not natural; it arises, like false ambition in men, from a love of power.

Dr. Gregory goes much further; he actually recommends dissimulation, advising an innocent girl to lie to her own feelings and not dance with spirit, when gaiety of heart would make her feet eloquent without making her gestures immodest. In the name of truth and common sense, why should one woman not acknowledge that she can take more exercise than another—or, in other words, that she has a sound constitution? And why should innocent vivacity be dampened by darkly warning her that men will draw conclusions she has not thought of? Let the libertine draw whatever inference he pleases; but I hope that no sensible mother will restrain the natural frankness of youth by instilling such indecent cautions. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh; and a wiser than Solomon has said that the heart should be made clean, rather than observing trivial ceremonies, which it is not very difficult to fulfill with scrupulous exactness when vice reigns in the heart.

Women ought to try to purify their hearts; but can they, when their uncultivated understandings make them entirely dependent on their senses for employment and amusement, when no noble pursuit raises them above the little vanities of the day, or enables them to curb the wild emotions that agitate a reed over which every passing breeze has power? To gain the affections of a virtuous man, is affectation necessary?

Nature has given woman a weaker frame than man; but in order to ensure her husband’s affections, must a wife who has, through exercise of mind and body while discharging the duties of daughter, wife, and mother, allowed her constitution to retain its natural strength and her nerves a healthy tone—must she, I say, condescend to use art, and feign a sickly delicacy, in order to secure her husband’s affection? Weakness may excite tenderness, and gratify the arrogant pride of man; but the lordly caresses of a protector will not gratify a noble mind that longs for, and deserves, respect. Fondness is a poor substitute for friendship!

In a seraglio, I grant, all these arts are necessary; the epicure must have his palate tickled, or he will sink into apathy; but have women so little ambition that they are satisfied with such a condition? Can they supinely dream life away in the lap of pleasure, or in the languor of weariness, rather than assert their claim to pursue reasonable pleasures, and distinguish themselves by practising the virtues that dignify mankind? Surely she has no immortal soul who can loiter through life merely occupied with adorning her person, so that she may amuse the languid hours and soften the cares of a fellow-creature willing to be enlivened by her smiles and tricks when the serious business of life is over.

Besides, the woman who strengthens her body and exercises her mind, by managing her family and practising various virtues, will become the friend, not the humble dependent, of her husband; and if she deserves his regard by possessing such substantial qualities, she will not need to conceal her affection, or to pretend to an unnatural coldness of constitution to excite her husband’s passions. In fact, if we look back through history, we find that the women who have distinguished themselves were neither the most beautiful nor the most gentle of their sex.

Nature, or to speak with strict propriety, God, has made all things right; but man has sought out many inventions to mar the work. I now allude to that part of Dr. Gregory’s treatise where he advises a wife never to let her husband know the extent of her sensibility or affection. Voluptuous precaution—and as ineffectual as it is absurd! Love, from its very nature, must be transient. To seek a secret that would make it constant would be as wild a quest as searching for the philosopher’s stone, or the grand panacea; and the discovery would be equally useless—or rather harmful—to mankind. The most holy bond of society is friendship. It has been well said, by a shrewd satirist, “that rare as true love is, true friendship is still rarer.”
This is an obvious truth, and since the cause does not lie deep, it will not escape a brief glance of inquiry.

Love, the common passion in which chance and sensation take the place of choice and reason, is felt to some degree by the mass of mankind; for there is no need at present to speak of the emotions that rise above or sink below love. This passion, naturally heightened by suspense and difficulty, draws the mind out of its accustomed state and exalts the affections; but with the security of marriage allowing the fever of love to subside, a healthy temperature seems insipid only to those who lack enough intellect to substitute the calm tenderness of friendship and the confidence of respect for blind admiration and the sensual emotions of fondness.

This is, and must be, the course of nature—friendship or indifference inevitably follows love. And this constitution seems perfectly to harmonize with the system of government that prevails in the moral world. Passions are spurs to action, and they open the mind; but they sink into mere appetites, becoming a personal momentary gratification, when the object is gained and the satisfied mind rests in enjoyment. The man who had some virtue while struggling for a crown often becomes a voluptuous tyrant when it sits on his brow; and when the lover is not lost in the husband, the dotard, prey to childish caprices and fond jealousies, neglects the serious duties of life, and the caresses that should inspire confidence in his children are lavished on the overgrown child, his wife.

In order to fulfill the duties of life and to be able to pursue with vigor the various employments that form moral character, a master and mistress of a family ought not to continue loving each other with passion. What I mean is that they ought not to indulge those emotions which disturb the order of society and engross thoughts that should be otherwise employed. The mind that has never been engrossed by one object lacks vigor—if it can long be so absorbed, it is weak.

A mistaken education, a narrow uncultivated mind, and many sexual prejudices tend to make women more constant than men; but I shall not touch on this branch of the subject at present. I will go further and assert, without dreaming of paradox, that an unhappy marriage is often very advantageous to a family, and that the neglected wife is generally the best mother. And this would almost always be the result, if the female mind were more enlarged; for it seems to be the common dispensation of Providence that what we gain in present enjoyment should be deducted from the treasure of life, experience; and that when we are gathering the flowers of the day and reveling in pleasure, the solid fruit of toil and wisdom should not be reaped at the same time. The way lies before us—we must turn to the right or to the left; and whoever spends life bounding from one pleasure to another must not complain if he acquires neither wisdom nor respectability of character.

Suppose for a moment that the soul is not immortal, and that man was created only for the present scene: I think we would have reason to complain that love, infantine fondness, ever grew insipid and palled upon the sense. “Let us eat, drink, and love, for tomorrow we die” would in fact be the language of reason, the morality of life; and who but a fool would part with a reality for a fleeting shadow? But if, awed by observing the improvable powers of the mind, we disdain to confine our wishes or thoughts to such a comparatively mean field of action—which appears grand and important only as it is connected with a boundless prospect and sublime hopes—what need is there for falsehood in conduct, and why must the sacred majesty of truth be violated to hold on to a deceitful good that saps the very foundation of virtue? Why must the female mind be tainted by coquettish arts to gratify the sensualist and prevent love from settling into friendship or compassionate tenderness, when there are no qualities on which friendship can be built? Let the honest heart show itself, and let REASON teach passion to submit to necessity; or let the dignified pursuit of virtue and knowledge raise the mind above those emotions that, when not restrained within proper bounds, embitter rather than sweeten the cup of life.

I do not mean to allude to the romantic passion that is the companion of genius. Who can clip its wings? But that grand passion, not proportioned to the puny enjoyments of life, is only true to the sentiment and feeds on itself. The passions that have been celebrated for their durability have always been unfortunate. They have gained strength by absence and constitutional melancholy. The fancy has hovered around a form of beauty dimly seen—but familiarity might have turned admiration into disgust, or at least into indifference, and allowed the imagination leisure to start fresh game. With perfect propriety, on this view of things, Rousseau makes Eloisa, the mistress of his soul, love St. Preux while life was fading before her; but this is no proof of the immortality of the passion.

Of the same character is Dr. Gregory’s advice about delicacy of sentiment, which he advises a woman not to acquire if she has determined to marry. This determination, however perfectly consistent with his previous advice, he calls INDELICATE, and earnestly urges his daughters to conceal it, even though it may govern their conduct—as if it were indelicate to have the common appetites of human nature.

Noble morality! And consistent with the cautious prudence of a little soul that cannot extend its views beyond the present minute division of existence. If all the faculties of woman’s mind are to be cultivated only as they relate to her dependence on man; if, when she obtains a husband, she has reached her goal, and is meanly proud and satisfied with such a paltry crown—let her grovel contentedly, scarcely raised by her employments above the animal kingdom. But if she is striving for the prize of her high calling, let her cultivate her understanding without pausing to consider what character the husband she is destined to marry may have. Let her resolve, without too much anxiety about present happiness, to acquire the qualities that ennoble a rational being, and a rough, inelegant husband may shock her taste without destroying her peace of mind. She will not model her soul to suit the frailties of her companion, but to bear with them: his character may be a trial, but not an impediment to virtue.

If Dr. Gregory had confined his remark to romantic expectations of constant love and congenial feelings, he should have remembered that experience will banish what advice can never make us cease to wish for, when the imagination is kept alive at the expense of reason.

I own it frequently happens that women who have fostered a romantic, unnatural delicacy of feeling waste their lives IMAGINING how happy they would have been with a husband who could love them with a fervent, ever-growing affection every day and all day long. But they might as well pine while married as while single, and would not be a jot more unhappy with a bad husband than longing for a good one. That a proper education—or, to put it more precisely, a well-stored mind—would enable a woman to support a single life with dignity, I grant; but that she should avoid cultivating her taste lest her husband should occasionally shock it, is giving up a substance for a shadow. To tell the truth, I do not know what use an improved taste is, if it does not render the individual more independent of the casualties of life, if new sources of enjoyment, dependent only on the solitary operations of the mind, are not opened. People of taste, whether married or single, will always be disgusted by various things that do not offend less observant minds. The argument must not be made to hinge on this conclusion; but in the whole sum of enjoyment, is taste to be called a blessing?

The question is whether it brings more pain or pleasure. The answer will decide the propriety of Dr. Gregory’s advice, and show how absurd and tyrannical it is to lay down a system of slavery in this way; or to try to educate moral beings by any other rules than those deduced from pure reason, which apply to the whole species.

Gentleness of manners, forbearance, and long-suffering are such amiable, godlike qualities that in sublime poetic strains the Deity has been invested with them; and perhaps no representation of his goodness so strongly fastens on the human affections as those that represent him abundant in mercy and willing to pardon. Gentleness, considered in this light, bears all the marks of grandeur, combined with the winning graces of condescension. But what a different aspect it takes on when it is the submissive demeanour of dependence, the support of weakness that loves because it needs protection; and is forbearing because it must silently endure injuries; smiling under the lash at which it dare not snarl. Abject as this picture is, it is the portrait of an accomplished woman, according to the accepted opinion of female excellence, separated by specious reasoners from human excellence. Or they (See Rousseau and Swedenborg) kindly restore the rib and make one moral being of a man and woman, not forgetting to give her all the “submissive charms.”

How women are to exist in that state where there is to be neither marrying nor giving in marriage, we are not told. For though moralists have agreed that the tenor of life seems to prove that MAN is prepared by various circumstances for a future state, they constantly concur in advising WOMAN only to provide for the present. Gentleness, docility, and a spaniel-like affection are, on this ground, consistently recommended as the cardinal virtues of the sex; and, disregarding the arbitrary economy of nature, one writer has declared that it is masculine for a woman to be melancholy. She was created to be the toy of man, his rattle, and it must jingle in his ears whenever, dismissing reason, he chooses to be amused.

To recommend gentleness on a broad basis is, indeed, strictly philosophical. A frail being should labour to be gentle. But when forbearance confounds right and wrong, it ceases to be a virtue; and however convenient it may be in a companion, that companion will always be considered an inferior, and will only inspire a vapid tenderness that easily degenerates into contempt. Still, if advice could really make a being gentle whose natural disposition did not admit of such fine polish, something toward the advancement of order would be gained; but if, as could quickly be demonstrated, only affectation is produced by this indiscriminate counsel, which throws a stumbling block in the way of gradual improvement and true betterment of temper, the sex is not much benefited by sacrificing solid virtues to the attainment of superficial graces, even though for a few years they may secure the individual’s regal sway.

As a philosopher, I read with indignation the plausible epithets men use to soften their insults; and as a moralist, I ask what is meant by such heterogeneous associations as fair defects, amiable weaknesses, etc.? If there is only one criterion of morals, only one archetype for man, women appear to be suspended by destiny, like Mahomet’s coffin in the vulgar tale; they have neither the unerring instinct of brutes, nor are they allowed to fix the eye of reason on a perfect model. They were made to be loved, and must not aim at respect, lest they should be hunted out of society as masculine.

But to view the subject from another angle. Do passive, indolent women make the best wives? Confining our discussion to the present moment of existence, let us see how such weak creatures perform their part. Do the women who, by attaining a few superficial accomplishments, have reinforced the prevailing prejudice, merely contribute to the happiness of their husbands? Do they display their charms merely to amuse them? And do women who have early absorbed notions of passive obedience have enough character to manage a family or educate children? So far from it, that after surveying the history of woman, I cannot help agreeing with the severest satirist, in considering the sex as both the weakest and the most oppressed half of the species. What does history reveal but marks of inferiority, and how few women have emancipated themselves from the galling yoke of sovereign man? So few that the exceptions remind me of an ingenious conjecture about Newton: that he was probably a being of a superior order, accidentally caged in a human body. In the same vein I have been led to imagine that the few extraordinary women who have rushed in eccentric directions out of the orbit prescribed for their sex were MALE spirits, confined by mistake in a female frame. But if it is not philosophical to think of sex when the soul is mentioned, the inferiority must depend on the organs; or the heavenly fire that ferments the clay is not given in equal portions.

But avoiding, as I have so far done, any direct comparison of the two sexes collectively, or frankly acknowledging the inferiority of woman according to the present appearance of things, I shall only insist that men have increased that inferiority until women are almost sunk below the standard of rational creatures. Let their faculties have room to unfold, and their virtues to gain strength, and then determine where the whole sex must stand in the intellectual scale. Yet, let it be remembered, that for a small number of distinguished women I am not asking a place.
